analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal compensation program paying firefighters with PFAS-linked cancers, funded by taxes on PFAS makers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a no-fault federal program paying firefighters who develop PFAS-related illnesses — $250,000 for a cancer, $50,000 for another covered illness, multiplied up to four times based on years of service. It would be funded by a new PFAS Trust Fund filled by a 10% excise tax on PFAS products (including firefighter gear) and a 10% tax on PFAS litigation settlements. Firefighters would not have to prove anyone was negligent; the program would presume their on-the-job exposure caused the illness.
analysis.who_benefits: Firefighters — career, military, and volunteer — with two or more years of service who develop PFAS-linked conditions such as kidney, testicular, thyroid, and other cancers, thyroid disease, or ulcerative colitis. Their heirs or estates could claim after a firefighter's death. Because the program is no-fault, they would not need to win a lawsuit proving which manufacturer's product harmed them; the government would presume their firefighting exposure caused the illness and pay within 120 days, with a right to a fresh court review on appeal. Awards scale with service: a firefighter with 10 or more years could receive up to $1 million for a cancer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Firefighters with PFAS-linked cancers and their families

how_it_helps.text: Creates a no-fault compensation program for firefighters with PFAS-related health conditions, so they would not have to sue chemical companies and prove which product made them sick — the Secretary of Health and Human Services must treat the illness as caused by on-duty PFAS exposure and may not consider negligence.

Sets base awards of $250,000 for a PFAS-linked cancer and $50,000 for a non-cancer condition, multiplied by a service modifier from 1 (2–5 years of service) to 4 (10 or more years), so a long-serving firefighter with cancer could receive up to $1 million.

Extends eligibility to the estates or adult heirs of firefighters who died from a PFAS-related condition, with written notice of decisions within 120 days and the right to appeal to the Court of Federal Claims, which would review the case fresh with new evidence allowed.

Covers a broad list of conditions linked to PFAS — cancers of the kidney, testicle, liver, prostate, bladder, pancreas, breast, colon, and ovary, plus thyroid diseases and ulcerative colitis — with an expert advisory panel empowered to add more illnesses over time.

Funds the program from a new PFAS Trust Fund financed by a 10% excise tax on PFAS products sold by manufacturers, producers, and importers — including firefighter gear — and a 10% excise tax on qualifying PFAS litigation awards, so the industry whose products caused the exposure pays rather than general taxpayers.
Caps attorneys' fees at the percentage allowed under 28 U.S.C. 2678 and prohibits charging more, with penalties for violators, so more of each award reaches the firefighter or family.

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers, producers, and importers would pay a new 10% excise tax on PFAS products sold, including firefighting gear. Companies paying PFAS-related litigation awards other than personal-injury claims would pay an additional 10% excise on those amounts. Some of the product tax would likely be passed through to buyers of PFAS-containing goods — including fire departments purchasing gear — and the tax on litigation awards would reduce the net value of PFAS settlements to their recipients. Federal administrative costs would be authorized to be appropriated for fiscal years 2025–2029.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS manufacturers and companies paying PFAS settlements

drawbacks.text: Payments could be prorated: the program must not spend more than the PFAS Trust Fund holds, so if tax revenue fell short of total claims, the Secretary would reduce payments and later pay the shortfall plus 6% annual interest — meaning sick firefighters might wait years for full awards.

The 10% excise tax on PFAS products would raise prices on goods containing the chemicals, including the very firefighter gear that causes the exposure, a cost partly borne by fire departments and other purchasers.

The program presumes any covered illness in a firefighter was caused by PFAS exposure and bars consideration of liability, which would compensate some claims where PFAS was not actually the cause; in exchange it also limits recovery to one cancer and one non-cancer condition per firefighter, excludes punitive damages, and allows only one claim per person.
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor in either party, which under normal practice signals no realistic path to consideration even if the Congress had continued.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For firefighters — a workforce with documented elevated rates of the cancers listed in the bill, exposure that comes from gear, foam, and fire scenes rather than personal choice — the tradeoff is a strong one: guaranteed payments without years of litigation, paid by taxes on the industry that made the chemicals. The honest costs are real but bounded: the funding depends on how much revenue the new excise taxes raise, so awards could be reduced and delayed if claims outpace the fund; the tax partly raises prices on PFAS-containing goods; and the no-fault presumption trades precision about causation for speed and certainty. The largest weakness is design-to-death: a compensation program this detailed arrived with zero cosponsors and no committee attention, so the merits were never weighed at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2024 and sent to three committees, but none of them ever held a hearing or a vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Darren Soto introduced the Firefighter PFAS Injury Compensation Act of 2024 on March 21, 2024.
The House referred it the same day to three committees — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Budget — a multi-committee referral that means any one panel could have kept it from moving.
It was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health the next day, which is the last action ever taken on the bill.
The bill drew no cosponsors during its nine months of life.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever held, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and other companies facing PFAS liability are better off because the bill died: the 10% excise taxes on their products and litigation settlements never materialized. Firefighters with PFAS-linked cancers gained nothing and remain dependent on suing manufacturers case by case.

sides.party_line_note: The partisan shape was never tested: the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party and no roll-call vote was ever held.

industries.note: The bill imposes a 10% excise tax on PFAS products they sell and a 10% excise tax on PFAS litigation awards they pay (other than personal-injury claims), while a no-fault compensation program would give firefighters an alternative to suing them. The bill died, so none of this took effect.

industries.industry: Makers of PFAS-containing goods, including firefighting gear and foam
industries.note: Their products would carry a 10% manufacturer-level excise tax, likely raising prices for fire departments and other purchasers. Gear is also the source of the firefighter exposure the bill aims to compensate.

industries.industry: Companies and insurers paying PFAS litigation settlements
industries.note: A 10% excise tax on the present value of qualifying PFAS litigation awards (excluding personal-injury claims) would come out of settlement money.
A no-fault federal program with capped fees would channel claims away from contingency litigation, though attorneys could still represent claimants within the fee cap and on appeal.
